title: Marx: Alienation
keyWorks: The German Ideology (1845–1846, with Friedrich Engels)
summary: As a young man, Karl Marx wrote manuscripts about how a person can become a stranger to themselves — "alienated". He believed that people come into their own through free, creative activity and through their connections with others, and that when work and life are arranged so that this is impossible, people suffer — and often think it is their own fault.
onEmotions: The young Marx saw the human being as a "species-being" — a creature that lives in connection with others and expresses itself through activity. For him feelings are not only inner states but also responses to how our life is arranged: work, money, relationships. Many painful experiences — tiredness, emptiness, loneliness, envy — can be linked to what he called "alienation": when labour, its results and other people become something external and alien to a person. It is an important idea: part of your pain may have not only personal but also social causes. It doesn't cancel your choices, but it lifts needless guilt.

anxiety.text: Marx compared modern society to a sorcerer who has summoned up powers from the underworld and can no longer control them. When the future feels shaky, anxiety is often the first to sense those powers. The young Marx described a situation in which a person depends on forces they don't control: the market, money, the decisions of distant people. In the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 he shows how what people have created begins to rule over them, like an alien power. Then part of your anxiety is a reasonable response to real uncertainty, not just "wrong thoughts" in your head. That can bring relief: you are not simply "too anxious a person" — you live in a world where much really doesn't depend on you. It helps to separate what is in your power from what is determined by circumstances, and not to shoulder the latter.
anxiety.practice: Step outside for five minutes and look at the city through Marx's eyes: who built this house, who is hauling this load, who decides what bread costs? For a moment your anxiety joins a long line — and you are not alone in it.

fear.text: "The reserve army of labour" — Marx's name for the people an economy keeps in waiting, whose very existence keeps everyone else on edge. If you are afraid of losing your footing, that fear was not invented by you. He saw people whose existence depends on things they have no power over: will there be work, will the money be enough, will you turn out to be "surplus"? In the 1844 manuscripts he bitterly remarks that the demand for people regulates their fate just as the demand for any other commodity does. So many fears — losing your job, not coping, being unneeded — come not from your weakness but from the way our shared life is organized. Understanding this doesn't remove the fear, but it makes it less lonely: a great many people share the same insecurity, and it is easier to bear when it can be talked about together.
fear.practice: Say one honest sentence to a colleague or a friend: "I'm afraid of this too." For Marx, solidarity begins when a shared fear is named out loud.

sadness.text: Marx dreamed of a person who recognizes themselves in what they make, as in a mirror: in bread, in a table, in a song. If you are sad and can't name why, perhaps it has been a long time since you saw that mirror. The young Marx believed that a person needs to express themselves fully: in activity, creativity, connection with others and with nature. He called this our "species-being" — what makes us human. When life is reduced to survival and obligations, this essence finds no outlet, and a person feels impoverished even if outwardly everything is fine. Then sadness is sometimes the voice of your unrealized humanity: the part of you that wants to do, to create and to be with others. It isn't a whim but a longing for a fuller life. It deserves to be heard, not drowned out.
sadness.practice: Today, make something small with your hands from start to finish: brew tea properly, sew on a button, slice bread. Look at the result — that's you, reflected in a thing.

grief.text: A few days after his eight-year-old son Edgar died, Marx wrote to Engels that he had known plenty of bad luck, but only now did he know what real misfortune is. If you have lost someone, those words are about you too. The young Marx also had an idea that explains a lot: the essence of a human being is the ensemble of their relationships with others. It follows that we are made of our connections, and when someone close to us leaves, part of us leaves too. Grief is an honest reflection of how deeply we are bound to others. In another letter he admitted that he was not one of those "great men" who bear any loss easily. It's a reminder: there is nothing unworthy in grief, even for the strongest minds.
grief.practice: Tell someone one story about the person you lost — a funny one or a very simple one. Marx saw the essence of a person in their relationships: as long as stories are told about them, those relationships go on.

loneliness.text: Even Robinson Crusoe on his island, Marx joked, keeps books on his time and goods like a true Englishman — he carries society inside him. Loneliness still hurts, but it points to a truth: you need people because you are made of them. The young Marx saw the human being as a deeply social creature: we become ourselves only through others. One of the forms of alienation he described is the alienation of person from person: when people meet mainly as competitors, buyers and sellers, performers of functions, rather than as living beings. So loneliness is not only your personal failure but also a consequence of how work, cities and the rhythm of life are arranged. That doesn't mean nothing can be done, but it takes away the shame. Marx dreamed of relationships in which people need each other as people, not as means.
loneliness.practice: Call or drop in on one person not "on business" — just to ask how their day went. Not as a colleague, a client or a service provider, but as one human being to another.

quote.text: But the essence of man is no abstraction inherent in each single individual. In its reality it is the ensemble of the social relations.
quote.author: Karl Marx

anger.text: Marx called the first volume of Capital the most terrible missile ever hurled at the heads of the bourgeoisie. His fury had a target — and your anger, too, most likely points at something unjust. The young Marx was sensitive to how people suffer from conditions they did not create. Part of your anger is a sober response to real pressure, inequality or humiliation, not a trait of your character. From his idea of the alienation of person from person one can draw a subtler observation, too: tension whose source lies in the very structure of life is often unloaded onto those nearby — a colleague, a neighbour, someone close. Understanding this frees both you and others from some unnecessary guilt. Anger doesn't need to be suppressed; it can be directed at what can actually be changed.
anger.practice: Take a brisk ten-minute walk and with each step sort it out silently: this person — or what is pressing on us both? By the end of the walk, name one thing that can actually be changed.

shame.text: In 1843 the young Marx wrote to Arnold Ruge that shame is a kind of anger turned inward. If you want to disappear right now, that line holds an unexpected clue. Shame is often the energy of disagreement that we have aimed at ourselves instead of seeing where it really belongs. Marx also showed how, in a society where a person's worth is measured by money and success, people begin to be ashamed of poverty, failure, "inefficiency". In the 1844 manuscripts he wrote that money can turn human qualities into their opposites. If your shame is about not earning or achieving "enough", it's worth asking: is this the truth about you, or about a yardstick the world has imposed on you?
shame.practice: Put a hand on your chest and ask your shame in a whisper: "Whose yardstick are you measuring me by?" Then send that anger back where it belongs — silently name the yardstick you don't agree with.

quote.text: Shame is a kind of anger which is turned inward.
quote.author: Karl Marx

guilt.text: In Capital Marx does the bookkeeping: who owes what to whom, and why. Try the same audit of your guilt — calmly, like an accountant, not like a judge. The young Marx showed that many of life's circumstances — lack of time, money, strength, work you're forced to do — are created not by one person but by the whole system of social relations. In the 1844 manuscripts he describes how a person in alienated labour controls neither their activity nor its fruits. Perhaps part of your guilt — for example, for not getting enough done, not caring or earning "enough" — may be guilt for things that weren't entirely up to you. This doesn't cancel responsibility where it truly is yours. But it helps you distinguish: where can I act differently, and where am I carrying someone else's load?
guilt.practice: Do an audit: write down what you blame yourself for and enter it in two columns — "my debt" and "the debt of circumstances". Sign at the bottom like an accountant: "Checked".

envy.text: "The less you are, the more you have" — Marx arrived at that bitter formula in Paris in 1844. It's worth recalling when someone else's wealth or success stings. The young Marx noticed that in a world where a person's status and worth are measured by property, envy becomes almost inevitable. In the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts he writes that private property breeds envy of the richer and a desire to "level everyone down". Interestingly, he considered this response immature: envy merely turns the same logic of "having" upside down without going beyond it. His ideal is not to "have more" but to "be" more fully: to develop your abilities, senses, relationships. Envy can hint at what you lack, but it's worth asking: do I need this to live more fully, or so as not to lose in comparison?
envy.practice: Imagine that what you envy could never be shown to anyone: no photo, no story. Would you still want it as much? What remains is your "being"; what vanished was "having".

emptiness.text: The worker puts his life into the object, Marx wrote, and then it belongs to the object, not to him. If you feel empty, perhaps too much of your life has gone where it doesn't come back from. The young Marx described alienation from one's own activity: when work is done not because it expresses you but only as a means of survival. In such labour, he wrote, a person does not freely develop their physical and mental energy but mortifies themselves. Emptiness often appears where we have long been doing things we don't feel are our own. It's not an emptiness inside you, but the trace of a gap between you and what fills your days. Marx believed that a person comes alive in "free, conscious activity". Even a small island of such activity can bring back a sense of being alive.
emptiness.practice: Give yourself ten minutes of "free, conscious activity" in miniature: do something no one asked for and no one will judge — fold a paper boat, repot a plant, pick out a tune. Notice when something in you stirs.

confusion.text: "All that is holy is profaned," Marx and Engels wrote in the Manifesto about a world where old rules collapse faster than new ones form. If you have lost your bearings, you are in good company. Confusion, then, is not a personal inability but a natural response to rapidly changing conditions of work, relationships and values. Marx also taught us to look at life historically: what seems "natural" and eternal actually took shape at a particular time and can change. That is liberating. If you feel confused, perhaps you have simply noticed that the familiar rules are not so unshakable after all. It's unpleasant, but it is also the beginning of a clearer view — and of your own choice.
confusion.practice: Read aloud: "All that is solid melts into air, all that is holy is profaned, and man is at last compelled to face with sober senses his real conditions of life." Then name one "that's how it's done" that confuses you, and ask: who invented it, and when?

fatigue.text: "The worker feels at home when he is not working, and when he is working he does not feel at home" — Marx wrote that in 1844, long before the word "burnout". If nothing of you is left by evening, he described you with striking precision. He called this "alienated labour": work that doesn't express a person but only drains their strength. Labour becomes external, forced, and all that remains after it is exhaustion. Burnout is not proof that you "can't handle it" but an understandable response to activity in which you yourself are barely present. This can lift some of the guilt: it isn't only about you. And it suggests a direction: protect the time in which you are "at home" in yourself, and look for something in your work that you can make your own.
fatigue.practice: Drop your shoulders, unclench your fingers and feel it: all day these hands belonged to tasks. Tell them out loud, "The shift is over," and for three long out-breaths do nothing at all.

quote.text: The worker therefore only feels himself outside his work, and in his work feels outside himself. He feels at home when he is not working, and when he is working he does not feel at home.
quote.author: Karl Marx
quote.source: Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, "Estranged Labour"

boredom.text: "An appendage of the machine" — that is what the Manifesto calls a person of whom only the simplest, most monotonous knack is required. The boredom draining you right now is a small revolt against that fate. Boredom is the protest of your many-sided nature against monotony. Marx believed that humans are by nature versatile: we want to think, to work with our hands, to talk with others and to create. So boredom is not your shortcoming but a hint: some part of you lacks room. In The German Ideology Marx and Engels even dreamed of a life in which one could hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon, rear cattle in the evening and criticize after dinner.
boredom.practice: Right now, put to work the part of you that has been bored the longest: your hands — mend or mould something; your head — solve a puzzle; your voice — sing a verse. Five minutes of many-sidedness.

joy.text: His children called Marx "the Moor" and rode on his back as if he were a horse. This was no ascetic — he would have taken your joy seriously. In the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts he writes that a person affirms themselves in the world through all their senses — sight, hearing, taste, love. These "human senses" develop together with culture: the musical ear, the eye that feels the beauty of form. Joy is a moment when your senses are alive at full strength: you truly see, hear, delight. Marx criticized a world in which the "sense of having" crowds out all the other senses. That is why joy unconnected with possession — from music, nature, an encounter — is especially precious: in it you are fully human.
joy.practice: Give one minute to one of the "human senses" Marx wrote about: only listen, or only look, without judging or buying anything. What do you notice that you hadn't noticed before?

quote.text: The forming of the five senses is a labour of the entire history of the world down to the present.
quote.author: Karl Marx

love.text: After thirteen years of exile and want, Marx wrote to his wife Jenny: "Love for you makes a man of me again." The tenderness you feel right now does the same. In the 1844 manuscripts, in the passage on the power of money, he shows how money substitutes for human qualities and relationships: you can get almost anything for it, but not real love. Against this he sets a way of life in which a person relates to the world and to others "humanly". Tenderness is the area of life where alienation retreats: you give not a function or a service, but yourself. For Marx love is one of the chief expressions of human essence, not a commodity. That is why your tenderness is valuable in itself, regardless of what it "brings in".
love.practice: Say one sentence to someone close "just because" — not a request or a report, but something you value in them. An exchange without gain is exactly Marx's "love for love".

quote.text: Assume man to be man and his relationship to the world to be a human one: then you can exchange love only for love, trust for trust, etc.
quote.author: Karl Marx
quote.source: Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, "The Power of Money"

gratitude.text: Coffee, the cotton of your shirt, the light in the lamp — Marx taught us to see in every thing the congealed labour of many people. The warmth you feel right now is the best way to notice it. He emphasized that the human being is a social creature: almost everything we have — language, knowledge, things, even our refined senses — was created by the labour of many other people. Even when you think alone, he wrote in the manuscripts, you use a language given to you by society, and your activity remains social. Gratitude is the recognition of an invisible web of people who support your life: those who grew the bread, built the house, taught you to read. Such gratitude doesn't diminish you, it connects you: you are part of a great shared undertaking.
gratitude.practice: Thank one invisible worker of your day out loud — a courier, a cleaner, a bus driver — or at least silently, looking at the fruit of their labour. Marx called this the social nature of human beings; you can simply call it "thank you".

hope.text: "Well grubbed, old mole!" — Marx, after Hamlet, used the phrase for changes that dig underground long before they show. If hope is flickering in you, perhaps it senses that mole. His idea of alienation contains a promise: what people have created, people can also change. If suffering flowed from "eternal human nature", there would be nothing to hope for. But if it is tied to how relationships, work and living conditions are arranged, then they can become different. Hope, then, is not a naive dream but an understanding that the world can change. It needn't be tied to great upheavals: hope begins where you see that even in your everyday life something is not "like this forever" but could be arranged differently.
hope.practice: Go outside and find three things that weren't here twenty years ago: a tree, a bench, a sign. The world changes the way a mole digs — unseen, and so does your life.

nostalgia.text: Every Sunday the Marx family in London walked to Hampstead Heath with a basket of food — his daughters remembered those outings all their lives. A warm ache for the past often clings to simple pictures like these. Marx would probably note that we often long not only for a time but for forms of life: a courtyard where everyone knew each other, work that was clear and your own, an unhurried pace. That is, for connections that rapid change has washed away. Marx didn't idealize the past — he saw both want and unfreedom in it. But his idea of an unalienated life helps you understand what is valuable in nostalgia: it points to what we truly need — closeness, meaningful work, your own mark on what you do. This can be sought not only behind you but in the present.
nostalgia.practice: Take a small "Hampstead" walk: spend ten minutes going somewhere that holds a piece of the rhythm you miss — a park, a market, an old street. Notice what from the past you can bring along into today.

craving.text: Everyone tries to create a new need in another, Marx wrote in 1844, so as to place them in a new dependence. When the pull hits "right now", that line reads almost like a manual for your phone — and there's nothing to be ashamed of. He noticed something strange: in a world where everything is for sale, needs aren't simply satisfied — they are produced. So part of your craving is not only "your weakness": the phone, the cigarette, the drink are designed and sold so that you'll be pulled back again. Marx set against such imposed needs the real ones — for activity, for connection, for being rather than having. A craving is a wave: it rises and falls. You can ride it out without arguing with yourself, and ask what real need it is trying to fill.
craving.practice: When a craving hits, set a timer for five minutes and watch it like the weather. Then ask: "Is this my need, or a manufactured one?" — and what you're really missing right now: rest, people, meaning.

addiction.text: "The opium of the people" — Marx's phrase about religion is usually quoted as mockery, but in the full text it sounds compassionate: "the sigh of the oppressed creature", a consolation in a world with too much pain. If your life has come to circle around one thing, that is not a moral failure but a hard circle. The same can be seen in addiction: what life came to be organized around was often a way of enduring something unbearable — loneliness, exhausting work, a sense of being unneeded. Marx added that to call for giving up illusions is to call for changing a condition that needs illusions. So the way out lies not in self-flagellation but in gradually reclaiming what was taken away: connections with people, work in which you recognize yourself.
addiction.practice: Say one sentence to one person — someone close, or a mutual-help group where people understand: "When it all began, it helped me endure…" Reclaiming what was taken is easier together with others.

quote.text: Religion is the sigh of the oppressed creature, the heart of a heartless world, just as it is the spirit of spiritless conditions. It is the opium of the people.
quote.author: Karl Marx
quote.source: A Contribution to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, Introduction (1844)

hangover.text: Marx wouldn't ask "how much did you drink?" but "what were you resting from last night?" Right now your body aches, and anxiety and shame pile on top — there's no need to scold yourself. The young Marx made a bitter observation: a person whose labour is alienated feels free almost only in the simplest functions — eating, drinking, resting — while in work, the most human of activities, they feel like a servant. A binge is often an attempt to win back at least a scrap of the freedom that's missing on ordinary days. But it doesn't give what the person is looking for, and in the morning the bill comes to you. This is not a verdict on your character but a reason to ask: where in your life could there be a freedom that doesn't hurt afterward?
hangover.practice: Drink a glass of water slowly, holding it in both hands, and gently ask yourself: "What was I resting from last night — and where can I find a freedom that doesn't hurt afterward?"

euphoria.text: Marx dreamed of a person who is "rich" not in money but in the need for a totality of human expressions of life. A burst in which everything seems possible lets you feel that wealth from the inside. Marx rarely wrote about such states directly, but in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts he describes what an unalienated person might be like: someone whose senses, abilities and connections with people are developed "in an all-round way", who lives rather than merely survives. In a moment of elation you glimpse this fullness of yours for a second: how much energy, desire and possibility there is in you. It's not an illusion but a reminder of what you are capable of. The high won't last forever. But you can keep it as knowledge: this is who I can be when nothing is squeezing me.
euphoria.practice: Take any receipt and on the back write down what exactly seems possible to you right now. Let your wallet carry an inventory of your real wealth — it'll come in handy on an ordinary day.

crash.text: Marx distinguished between the time a person sells and the time that belongs to them. When the celebration or success is over and the world seems to fade, you are feeling the seam between those two times. Marx would probably explain it like this: a celebration is a time when a person is briefly "at home" in themselves, and then returns to a routine in which they themselves are barely present. The contrast between these two worlds is what makes the comedown hurt. Marx saw the problem not in the fact that celebrations end, but in the fact that ordinary life can be arranged so poorly. So you can take the comedown as information: it shows the gap between what you want and how your everyday life is set up. That gap can be narrowed little by little.
crash.practice: Imagine that tomorrow's ordinary day is yours rather than sold: with which grain of that high — lightness, company, laughter — would you begin it? Save that grain for the morning.

panic.text: Marx always began with the material: a body that breathes, the floor under your feet, the things around you. If your heart is pounding and your breath is faltering right now, let's begin there too. First, the main thing: a wave like this usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Marx, of course, didn't write about panic attacks. But he would notice this: many people live in constant insecurity — about work, money, housing — and for years the body holds that background alarm signal. Marx described how social relations a person didn't choose become an alien, uncontrollable power over them. Panic is not proof that you are "weak". Sometimes it is a body that has been on alert for too long. Right now what matters most is not analysis but support: the ground under your feet, the out-breath, the objects around you.
panic.practice: Put both feet on the floor and press your palms against something solid — a table, a wall. Make your out-breath longer than your in-breath, and name aloud five things around you that someone's hands made.

dread.text: Who else is holding this thread besides you? — Marx would ask. The thought of finitude and the question "what's the point of it all" can close over your head, and then it seems you stand alone at the edge. The young Marx touched on this theme in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts. He wrote that death seems a harsh victory of the species over the particular individual — but added that each of us is part of that species, a "species-being". This means your life is woven into a vast human fabric: the language you speak, the things others have made, what you pass on. The answer to "what for?" is then sought not alone, inside your head, but in connections: in activity that someone else needs, in relationships. The abyss doesn't disappear, but many hands turn out to be near it.
dread.practice: Look around and find three things made by other people that hold up your life today — a chair, a lamp, a book. Touch each one: these are threads of that shared fabric.

fomo.text: "Commodity fetishism" — Marx's name for the spell under which a thing seems to radiate value all by itself. If other people's feeds look like life right now and yours like a rough draft, you are under the same spell. A feed of other people's trips, parties and purchases sells not life but an image of it — packaged like a commodity. Marx also set "having" against "being": the more we measure ourselves by possessions, the poorer we feel. Fear of missing out is not a personal deficiency but a natural response to an environment that deliberately shows you other people's abundance. Real life, for Marx, lies in what you do and with whom, not in what can be seen from outside.
fomo.practice: Live the next ten minutes so that they can't be posted: no photo, no story, no witnesses. Just look out of the window or sit with a cup of tea — the spell weakens when life stops being a shop window.

sleepless.text: Capital, Marx wrote, "usurps the time for growth, development and healthy maintenance of the body". If you're lying awake going over tasks, it may have taken this night too — but not for good. He noted that capital tends to reduce even healthy sleep to the minimum needed just to work again tomorrow. Night-time thoughts about work, money and unfinished tasks are not personal disorganization but a trace of how hard it is today to draw a line between work time and your own time. Your sleep is your time, and you have a right to it. You don't have to solve everything at night; it's enough to set your thoughts aside until morning.
sleepless.practice: Say to yourself: "The working day is over; this night is mine." Then turn your attention to the weight of the blanket and the warmth of the pillow, and with each out-breath set one unfinished task aside until morning.

betrayal.text: For forty years Marx and Engels trusted each other with money, manuscripts and secrets — a rare example of loyalty in history. When trust collapses, as it has for you, the worth of such loyalty stands out sharply. In the Manifesto Marx bitterly described how the market era "drowned" many human bonds "in the icy water of egotistical calculation", leaving no other bond between people than naked self-interest. And in the 1844 manuscripts he dreamed of a world where "trust can be exchanged only for trust". When you are betrayed, two logics often collide — the logic of relationship and the logic of gain, fear, competition. This doesn't excuse the act and doesn't oblige you to forgive. But it helps you avoid concluding that no one can be trusted. Your ability to trust is not naivety but the very human bond that Marx considered the greatest wealth.
betrayal.practice: Name one person whose trust in you, and yours in them, is still alive — and send them a short sign: "Thank you for being there." Trust, Marx wrote, can be exchanged only for trust.

jealousy.text: "Stupid and one-sided" — that, for Marx, is what private property has made us: an object seems ours only when we possess it. When jealousy burns, that voice of ownership sounds especially loud, and painful. Jealousy partly speaks the language of property: "he's mine", "she's mine". But the person you love is not a thing but a living subject with their own freedom. Marx considered truly human a relationship in which love can be exchanged only for love. That doesn't mean your jealousy is wrong or that you should be ashamed of it. It shows how dear the person is to you. It's just that you can place another question beside it: not "how do I hold on?" but "what is alive between us?"
jealousy.practice: Say one jealous thought out loud without the word "mine". What remains when you speak about the person rather than about ownership?

quote.text: Private property has made us so stupid and one-sided that an object is only ours when we have it.
quote.author: Karl Marx

resentment.text: Who else was in that room besides you and the one who hurt you? Marx would start with that question. An old wound quiets down for years and flares up again, and almost always there was real injustice behind it. In the preface to Capital Marx made an important caveat: he treats people as "personifications" of economic relations, and so is least of all inclined to hold the individual responsible for relations whose creature he remains. So part of what hurt you came not only from a particular person's ill will but also from the situation — the hierarchy, need, pressure within which they acted. This doesn't relieve them of responsibility and doesn't require forgiveness. But sometimes it helps to see the wider picture — and loosen a little the knot you are holding alone.
resentment.practice: Imagine that scene as a play and place the invisible participants on stage: the boss offstage, the lack of money, fear, the rules. Don't decide anything — just see how many people were on that stage.

heartbreak.text: At nineteen, the future author of Capital filled three notebooks with love poems for Jenny. If it hurts so much right now that it's hard to breathe, he would understand you. The young Marx wrote about love with a tenderness surprising in an economist. In the 1844 manuscripts he says that in a human world love can be exchanged only for love, and if your love does not call forth love in return, it is powerless — a "misfortune". It matters that he calls it a misfortune, not a disgrace. Rejection or a breakup doesn't prove you are "not good enough"; love can't be earned like a salary, and it can't be bought — that is its human dignity. Your pain is evidence that you treated the other as a person, not as a function. That is valuable, even when right now it only hurts.
heartbreak.practice: Read aloud slowly: "Love can be exchanged only for love." And add in your own words: "My love was real, and the ability to love is still mine." What answers in your chest?

impostor.text: Who set the price on your work, and why trust the price tag more than your own hands? Marx would ask. The fear of being "exposed" is agonizing and mostly visits the conscientious. Marx described how, in alienated labour, a person loses their connection to the result of their work: the product becomes alien, as if someone else had made it. Impostor syndrome partly comes from here: when the value of your work is determined by the market, by bosses, by metrics, it's hard to feel it as your own and to believe you've earned it. The market also constantly demands that you prove you're "worth" your price — and that pressure is easy to mistake for an inner truth about yourself. It helps to reconnect with the process: to remember what exactly you did with your own hands and head.
impostor.practice: Hold the result of some recent work — a file, a notebook, an object — and name aloud three actions that you yourself did. No judging: just return the product to its producer.

self_hatred.text: "And who are you working for?" — that is what Marx would ask the inner critic. When that voice insists you're worthless, it hurts, and it's wrong, however convincing. The young Marx wrote that under alienation a person becomes a stranger not only to their labour but to themselves. A society that measures people by productivity, price and success easily plants a strict appraiser inside us. The inner critic often speaks not in your voice but in the voice of the market: "you didn't do enough", "not efficient enough", "you're losing to others". Marx believed a person is valuable as a living being able to feel, create and be with others — not as a commodity. You don't have to win the argument with your inner critic; it's enough to notice that its yardsticks are borrowed and that you are more than its report.
self_hatred.practice: Say your inner critic's most frequent phrase out loud, then ask it in the same tone: "Who's paying you for this assessment?" Notice how the voice loses confidence when asked about its employer.

helplessness.text: People make their own history, Marx wrote in 1852, but not as they please — in circumstances they did not choose. He wrote it after the defeat of a revolution he had believed in, and knew from the inside the feeling that nothing depends on you. Both halves of the sentence matter. The first reminds you: you are not nothing, your actions mean something. The second lifts needless guilt: if you can't change everything, that's not your personal failure — the circumstances really are strong. Helplessness can be accepted as an honest acknowledgment of limits rather than a verdict. Within those limits there almost always remains something small that can be done — especially together with others.
helplessness.practice: Find one person who is troubled by the same thing — a neighbour, a colleague, a friend — and ask: "What could the two of us do, even the smallest thing?" The powerlessness of one and of two are different things.

quote.text: Men make their own history, but they do not make it as they please; they do not make it under self-selected circumstances, but under circumstances existing already, given and transmitted from the past.
quote.author: Karl Marx
quote.source: The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte (1852)

procrastination.text: As soon as compulsion disappears, people flee alienated labour like the plague, Marx wrote back in 1844. If you are putting off the same task for the tenth time, it isn't laziness, even though that's what we're taught to call it. Procrastination is often an honest response to a task in which you yourself are absent: the meaning is unclear, the result belongs to someone else, the control is in other hands. That doesn't mean the task doesn't need doing. But it changes the question from "what's wrong with me?" to "what makes this task feel so alien?" Sometimes it's enough to find even a small piece of yourself in it — your own method, your own order, your own interest.
procrastination.practice: Find one decision in the task that belongs only to you: which end to start from, in what order, to what music. Take the first, smallest step your own way — let it carry your handwriting.

quote.text: Its alien character emerges clearly in the fact that as soon as no physical or other compulsion exists, labour is shunned like the plague.
quote.author: Karl Marx
quote.source: Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, "Estranged Labour"

uprooted.text: Expelled from Prussia, expelled from Paris, expelled from Brussels — Marx spent his last thirty-four years in London as a stateless man, often in poverty. Lost footing, a foreign language, the sense of "I don't belong here" were well known to him. In the Manifesto he described an era in which all that is solid and familiar melts away, and people are compelled to face with sober senses their conditions of life and their relations with one another. Your feeling is not a personal failure to adapt but an experience the modern world imposes on millions. And Marx's thesis about the human being as the "ensemble of social relations" suggests: home is first of all connections. They can be grown again little by little, without giving up the old ones.
uprooted.practice: Walk around your new place and find something familiar by its craft: a bakery, a workshop, a market. Nod to it silently as to an old acquaintance — connections begin with recognition.

overload.text: Marx considered time a person's real wealth: "economy of time — to this all economy ultimately reduces itself". When your attention is torn to pieces and the feed never ends, that wealth leaks away unnoticed — and it's not your inability to "stay focused". Marx, of course, never saw a smartphone, but he described a logic you can recognize here: capital needs to keep expanding, turning ever new areas of life into commodities. Today your attention itself has become a commodity — it is collected, held and sold, and the feed is designed never to end. Marx also wrote that a person is alienated when the product of their activity begins to dominate them. Your minutes spent in the feed turn into someone else's profit. Understanding this lifts some of the guilt and gives back the right to say: my attention is mine, and I can protect it.
overload.practice: Put your phone in another room for ten minutes and simply sit, looking at something still. These are ten minutes that no one has bought or sold.

unreality.text: A simple thing — a table, a coin — turns out, in Marx's words, to be full of "metaphysical subtleties and theological niceties". If everything around you, or you yourself, feels unreal right now, it's strange and frightening; treat yourself gently. Relations between people, he wrote in Capital, take on before our eyes the "fantastic form" of relations between things. The world of prices, brands and screens has, in his words, a phantom-like objectivity. The sense of unreality is sometimes linked to living in an environment where much really is mediated and abstract. The way back to the real, for Marx, is the way back to living activity and living people: to what can be touched, made, shared.
unreality.practice: Pick up a simple object and name aloud its weight, temperature and texture. Then picture the hands that made it: behind the thing, people show through again.

awe.text: When Marx wanted to say the most important thing about nature, he called it the human being's "inorganic body": mountains and sea as an extension of ourselves. The awe that takes your breath away right now is rare and precious, and worth savoring. He also wrote that the human senses — the ability to see beauty, to hear music — are not given once and for all but were formed by the whole history of humankind. So your awe before mountains, the sea, a starry sky or a great work is not only a personal impression. Echoing in it is the long labour of countless people who taught the human eye and ear to feel this way. You can simply accept the wonder: in this moment you are living that full, unalienated feeling Marx dreamed of.
awe.practice: Stay one more minute and look as if this were part of your body, an extension of your hands and eyes. Then think about whom you'd like to share it with.

relief.text: In the third volume of Capital Marx distinguishes the "realm of necessity" — everything that has to be done to survive — from the "realm of freedom", which begins where need recedes. When something heavy lets go and you can finally breathe out, you cross the border between them for a moment. Allow yourself this feeling fully, without reservations and without hurry. Marx believed free time was the main condition for human development. The pressure has gone, and once again you have a space that belongs to you. This is neither trivial nor idleness, but what is worth saving your strength for. Don't rush to fill that space with new obligations right away.
relief.practice: Declare ten minutes of the "realm of freedom": no tasks from your list, no purchases, no messages. Notice where you are drawn when no one demands anything.

calm.text: Marx would ask of your calm: who don't you have to be right now? In this stillness you want to keep, there is nothing that needs justifying. In The German Ideology Marx and Engels sketched a utopian image: in a free society one could hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon, rear cattle in the evening and criticize after dinner, without ever becoming a hunter, fisherman or critic. The point of this picture is not agriculture but freedom: a person isn't chained to one role and lives in their own rhythm. Your calm is a moment when, briefly, you are not reduced to a function — worker, performer, debtor. You simply are. This experience is valuable in itself and reminds you what life could be like.
calm.practice: Tell yourself quietly: "Right now I am not a worker, not a performer, not a debtor." Stay for a minute in this time that belongs to no one, noticing your breath and the sounds around you.

inspiration.text: Milton wrote Paradise Lost the way a silkworm produces silk — that was Marx's image of labour that isn't for sale. What is burning in you right now and asking to come out is that same silkworm nature. You want to make, invent, create, and that is wonderful. The young Marx saw creative activity as the very essence of the human being. He wrote that a human, unlike an animal, creates "according to the laws of beauty", and that in free labour a person recognizes themselves in what they have made. Inspiration is a moment of unalienated activity, when you do something because it is yours. There's no need to "monetize" it or judge it right away. You can simply allow yourself to create.
inspiration.practice: Give your inspiration ten minutes "silkworm style": a sketch, a melody, a line — with no purpose, no judgment and no thought of whether it'll be useful.

quote.text: Milton produced Paradise Lost for the same reason that a silk worm produces silk. It was an activity of his nature.
quote.author: Karl Marx

schadenfreude.text: On a race track, someone else's fall looks like your chance — and Marx saw the market turning all of life into a race track. This small glee doesn't make you a bad person. In the 1844 manuscripts the young Marx described the "estrangement of man from man": when life is set up as constant competition — for a position, a salary, attention — the other person inevitably starts to look like a rival rather than a comrade. Schadenfreude is often born not of your "wicked nature" but of a logic in which someone else's success feels like your loss and someone else's failure like a small win. You might notice: the joy lasts a moment, and underneath it there is usually weariness from endless comparison. And you might ask yourself in what kind of world you wouldn't have to compete with this person.
schadenfreude.practice: Imagine a world in which you don't have to compete with this person — not for a position, not for attention. What would you feel toward them there? Stay with that picture for a minute.

contempt.text: In the parlour questionnaire "Confession", given to him by his daughters, Marx named "Nothing human is alien to me" as his favourite maxim and servility as the vice he detested most. The chill of contempt, so hard to admit to yourself, seems to have been familiar to him too. This suggests an interesting move: contempt sometimes points to a value that has been offended — dignity, honesty, a refusal to grovel. But Marx also showed something else: a society where people are ranked by money and status teaches us to look down on others, or up at them. It's worth asking whether your contempt is speaking in someone else's voice — the voice of that hierarchy. Contempt can be taken as a signal without turning it into a verdict on a person.
contempt.practice: Complete the sentence: "What I despise in them is… because what matters to me is…" What is that value?

disgust.text: "Dripping from head to foot, from every pore, with blood and dirt" — that's how Marx described the birth of capital, and you can hear disgust in it. Your feeling is the same ancient bodily "no, I don't want to touch this", and he would take it seriously. The young Marx wrote a great deal about the human senses: he believed our sight, taste and sense of beauty are fruits of a long history, and that under alienated conditions they grow coarse. Disgust at certain situations — at falseness, at work where only the numbers count, at humiliating rules — can be a sign of a living, unspoiled sensibility. And if the disgust is aimed at yourself, it's worth asking: are you looking at yourself through the eyes of the market, as a "defective product"? You are not a product. Disgust points to where you are missing something human.
disgust.practice: Notice where disgust lives in your body — throat, stomach, hands — and put a palm there. Ask: "What human quality is being violated here?"

revenge.text: In the preface to Capital Marx makes a caveat: he deals with individuals only insofar as they personify social relations. When you long for revenge, that caveat sounds almost provocative: a particular person hurt you, and your pain demands justice. This feeling doesn't make you cruel. And yet behind the one who hurt you there often stands a whole system of pressures, rules and roles, and revenge against one particular person rarely touches the real cause. This is not an excuse for the offender. It is a way of seeing that you don't have to carry your pain as a personal score to settle. You can hear the desire for revenge as a demand for justice — and look for ways to pursue it that don't multiply harm.
revenge.practice: Say out loud — ideally to someone you trust: "My hurt demands…" — and finish with one word: recognition, justice, safety. One word is already an answer.

anger_at_loved.text: Who else was sitting at your table during that fight? Marx would name the invisible guests: tiredness, debt, lack of time. Anger at family is frightening and brings shame afterwards, but you are not a bad person because it arises. Marx wrote little about family life in a psychological sense, but an important observation follows from his thought: the tiredness, lack of time and money worries that build up during the day don't stay at work — they come home. So part of the anger that crashes down on your family is actually addressed to the pressure you live under together. This doesn't cancel responsibility for your words, but it lifts needless self-blame and helps you talk to those close to you as allies.
anger_at_loved.practice: After an outburst, step into another room or onto the balcony for a minute and take three slow out-breaths. Then silently name two "invisible guests" that were pressing on you today before that moment.

ambivalence.text: "Contradiction is the root of all movement and vitality" — Marx took this thought of Hegel's and made it his own. Loving someone and being unable to stand them at once is hard, but by this logic entirely human. Things and relationships contain opposites, and development proceeds through their tension, not by eliminating one side. So mixed feelings toward someone close are not a sign that the love is "not real". They reflect the real contradictoriness of the relationship: it holds warmth and dependence, care and burden. You don't have to choose which feeling is "right". You can acknowledge both — and see in their clash a question about how the relationship might change.
ambivalence.practice: Draw two columns: "what I love in them" and "what I can't stand in them". Cross nothing out, then ask like a dialectician: what third thing could grow out of their argument?

guilty_relief.text: Watches at the bedside, medicines on the hour, sleepless nights — all of this is labour, though it's rarely called that. If after a death, a breakup or the end of a loved one's long illness you feel relief and it frightens you, know this: relief and love can live together perfectly well. Marx showed how much of human life is spent on hard, exhausting labour. Later thinkers building on him drew attention to the invisible labour of care — nursing the sick, giving support, keeping watch — which hardly anyone counts as work. Your relief is not a betrayal but a natural response of body and soul to the end of an enormous, often overwhelming load. It speaks of how much you carried, not of how little you loved. You can allow yourself both to grieve and to breathe out.
guilty_relief.practice: Draw up a timesheet of the invisible shift: write down what you carried all this time — tasks, worries, sleepless nights. Look at it as a term served, with respect for yourself.

indifference.text: "The care-burdened, needy man has no sense for the finest spectacle," Marx wrote in 1844. If where something "should" move you it's quiet and empty inside, that's frightening, but it doesn't make you heartless. Marx looked for the cause not in character but in conditions. Feelings are not a constant given: they grow dull when life is reduced to survival, to endless tasks and anxieties. Indifference is often not a character trait but a sign of depletion, the psyche's way of protecting itself from overload. You don't need to shame yourself for "wrong" reactions. It's better to ask how much strength and time you have right now simply to feel. The capacity to respond usually returns when a little room appears.
indifference.practice: Give yourself five minutes in which you don't have to feel anything: sit by the window and just look. Room for feelings begins with room in which nothing is expected of you.

quote.text: The care-burdened, poverty-stricken man has no sense for the finest play.
quote.author: Karl Marx

escape.text: Who are you tired of being? That's the question Marx would start with. The wish to drop your job, your city, your familiar role says something important in itself. In The German Ideology Marx and Engels dreamed of a society where a person isn't chained to one narrow function: where one could hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon and criticize in the evening, without becoming a "hunter" or a "critic" forever. The picture is deliberately simple, and many scholars see some irony in it, but the thought behind it is deep: a person feels cramped in a single role imposed on them. Your wish to escape may be a longing for a many-sided life. You don't have to change anything right away. First you can listen for which part of you lacks room.
escape.practice: Run a thought experiment in the spirit of The German Ideology: sketch tomorrow as "in the morning…, in the afternoon…, in the evening…", with at least one slot that isn't your usual role. Which of these is possible this week?

quote.text: …to hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon, rear cattle in the evening, criticise after dinner, just as I have a mind, without ever becoming hunter, fisherman, herdsman or critic.
quote.author: Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels

forbidden_attraction.text: Passion, the young Marx wrote, is the essential power of a human being energetically bent on its object. Attraction to someone who is "off limits" is confusing and unsettling, but the feeling itself doesn't yet decide anything about you. The young Marx treated human passions without moralizing: he saw the human being as a sensuous, "suffering" being — that is, one who needs the outer world and other people. Attraction is not a vice but a sign that you are alive and in need of something. It helps to ask what it is really reaching for: this particular person, or something missing from your life — aliveness, recognition, freedom. Understanding doesn't commit you to any action. It simply gives you back your own feeling.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Name three words to yourself: what you feel near this person. Then ask where else in your life at least one of these powers — aliveness, recognition, freedom — could live.

quote.text: Passion is the essential power of man energetically bent on its object.
quote.author: Karl Marx

social_anxiety.text: Shop window, price tag, buyer — Marx showed how, in a world where everything becomes a commodity, people come to feel that they themselves are up for sale. If it's frightening to go among people and wait for their verdict, that is heavy and draining, and you're not alone in it. Erich Fromm, who developed Marx's ideas, later called this the "marketing orientation": a person experiences themselves as a commodity whose value depends on how others "rate" them. Your fear of judgment is not only a personal weakness but also a reflection of an atmosphere of constant selection — interviews, likes and ratings. You are not goods in a shop window. In human relationships, Marx wrote, trust is exchanged only for trust, not for a successful "self-presentation".
social_anxiety.practice: Before a meeting, tell yourself: "I'm not going there to sell myself, just to be among people." Take off the imaginary price tag — and notice what changes in your shoulders and breathing.

uncertainty.text: "Doubt everything" was Marx's answer when asked for his favourite motto. When you're living without firm ground and don't know what comes next, that motto may sound like mockery — but there is comfort in it too. In the Manifesto Marx and Engels described the modern era as a time of continuous change, when nothing stays the same for long: professions, cities, the familiar way of life. Your insecurity is not only a personal inability to "plan everything" but a feeling the era itself produces in millions of people. That can ease the load a little: you are not obliged to single-handedly create a stability the world doesn't provide. Perhaps uncertainty can be met not only with fear but with questions: what here depends on me, and what doesn't?
uncertainty.practice: Walk for five minutes and at every crossing ask yourself: "Does this depend on me — or not?" Pick one thing from the first category and do it today.

quote.text: Constant revolutionising of production, uninterrupted disturbance of all social conditions, everlasting uncertainty and agitation distinguish the bourgeois epoch from all earlier ones.
quote.author: Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels

waiting.text: Marx has an image: the product of labour leaves the worker and lives its own life in other people's hands. When you are waiting for an answer, results or a decision, that's exactly what you're going through: time drags, and there's nothing you can do. It is truly agonizing. The heaviness of waiting is also a feeling of powerlessness: you put yourself in, and now the outcome is in someone else's hands — a committee, an employer, an institution. This is not your weakness but a very real dependence. But waiting doesn't have to swallow all your time. Marx valued free activity in which a person recognizes themselves. You can reclaim at least a small piece of time that belongs only to you.
waiting.practice: While the waiting lasts, go out for a ten-minute walk without your phone. The outcome is in other hands, but these ten minutes are in yours, and they answer to no one.

regret.text: "The tradition of all dead generations weighs like a nightmare on the brains of the living," Marx wrote. Your own past decisions can weigh like that too, coming back again and again, and that shows you care. Marx wrote that people make their own history, but not as they please — rather in circumstances they did not choose. Your past decisions were made not in a vacuum but under the pressure of money, time, others' expectations and what you knew then. Looking back, we see the choice more clearly than we saw it at the time, and we judge ourselves as if the circumstances hadn't existed. Honestly acknowledging them doesn't mean letting yourself off entirely. It means looking at your past as fairly as you would look at someone else's.
regret.practice: Imagine a historian telling the story of that decision impartially: which three circumstances would they be sure to mention? Say them aloud — the way you would about someone else's past.

longing.text: Human wealth, the young Marx wrote, is measured by how far another person — precisely as a person, not as a use or a function — has become a need for us. By that measure, your longing for one particular face is a sign of great wealth, even if right now it hurts. There is nothing shameful in it. What you miss is not services or comforts but this very face, this voice, this way of laughing. Marx believed the essence of a human being lies in their connections with others. So when someone isn't near, it's as if part of you is missing. Longing is the price of real closeness. It doesn't need to be hurried; it can be carried gently.
longing.practice: Say this person's name aloud, and one trait of theirs you came to know only through closeness. Stay with it for a minute — it is the wealth you share.

world_pain.text: The eleventh thesis on Feuerbach — "philosophers have only interpreted the world; the point is to change it" — is carved on Marx's gravestone in Highgate Cemetery. When grim news, violence and injustice hurt you, that line can press on you, as if you had to fix everything. The young Marx called the human being a "species-being": we are connected to all of humanity, and the suffering of others resonates in us for a reason. Your pain is not "excessive sensitivity" but an expression of that shared human bond. But no one can change the world alone and in a day. You can carry your part: help a particular person, do something kind nearby. And also protect your strength, so that the pain doesn't turn into burnout. Compassion needs rest, too.
world_pain.practice: Choose one small kind act for someone near you — and afterward allow yourself to put the news aside for at least an hour.

rejection.text: Fits, doesn't fit: Marx showed how the market sorts people like goods in a warehouse. When you've been turned down — for a job, a friendship, a love — it wounds deeply. In a world where people are constantly being selected, it's easy to start treating a refusal as a verdict on your worth. On the job market a rejection often means only that you didn't fit a narrow function, not that you as a person are not good enough. The logic of "selection" carries over into personal life too, and then every "no" feels like an assessment of your whole personality. But a person can't be reduced to the function someone is looking for in them. Marx believed in the richness of human abilities, many of which have no market price at all.
rejection.practice: Name aloud three of your qualities that have no market price and nothing to do with this rejection: a sense of humour, loyalty, the ability to listen. Say them slowly, like an inventory of real wealth.

abandonment.text: Marx called the essence of a human being "the ensemble of social relations": we are knots in a net, not separate dots. When the thought of being left frightens you, that deep, almost childlike fear deserves gentleness. Marx criticized the idea of the human being as an isolated individual, a "Robinson Crusoe" existing on their own. He believed humans are by nature social beings and simply cannot live fully outside their connections with others. Your fear is a reflection of a truth about people: we really do need one another. But there is also a social side: in a world where people are disconnected and support often rests on one or two close people, the fear of losing them becomes especially sharp. You can gradually widen your circle of support — not instead of the person close to you, but alongside them.
abandonment.practice: Send a short message to one person from your "second circle" — not the main one, but someone else who holds up your net: "Thought of you — how are you?" There are more knots in the net than it seems.

unrequited.text: Money, Marx wrote, can turn the ugly into the beautiful and the coward into the brave — but there is one thing it cannot buy. If you love without being loved back, your pain is real, and this is exactly about that thing. The young Marx has a famous passage on love: in a human world love can be exchanged only for love, trust only for trust. Marx acknowledged that love which calls forth no love in return becomes a misfortune for the one who loves. But a consolation follows from his thought too: the absence of a response doesn't mean you aren't trying "enough" or aren't worth something. Love doesn't obey the logic of merit and payment. Your capacity to love is a precious human power, and it remains yours even when this person can't respond.
unrequited.practice: Read aloud to yourself: "My love was not a payment, and a refusal is not an invoice for my worth." What do you feel, hearing it in your own voice?

humiliation.text: Asked for his idea of misery in the "Confession" questionnaire, Marx answered: "To submit." If you were humiliated in front of others, as if stripped of your dignity, it is not your fault. It hurts as if you had been turned into a thing. He was sensitive to how hierarchies of power and money allow some people to treat others as things. Humiliation speaks not of your insignificance but of an imbalance of power in a situation where you weren't recognized as an equal. It hurts precisely because you feel that a human being must not be treated this way. That feeling is your dignity, which goes on living even when it isn't recognized.
humiliation.practice: Tell yourself aloud: "I must not be treated this way." Straighten your back and notice where in your body that right resonates.

body_shame.text: Alienated labour, the young Marx wrote, makes even a person's own body alien to them: a tool rather than a living part of themselves. If you look in the mirror and see not yourself but a list of flaws, that is a very common and painful story. Today the body often becomes a "commodity" as well, a shop window constantly compared with models from advertising and social media. Beauty standards are largely created by a market that profits from your dissatisfaction. Marx saw the human being as a sensuous creature whose body is there for living, feeling and touching the world — not for matching a shop window. Your body is not an improvement project but your way of being alive.
body_shame.practice: Rest your palms on the part of your body you criticize most, and thank it for one thing it did for you today: carried, held, felt. A body is not a shop window but a way of being alive.

illness.text: Marx finished the first volume of Capital tormented by carbuncles, liver trouble and insomnia — and joked that the bourgeoisie would remember his carbuncles until their dying day. When your body lets you down, the ground slips away, and you have every right to grieve your former strength. The young Marx emphasized that the human being is a natural, bodily and vulnerable creature, not a machine. He described with bitterness how society values a person by their capacity to work, by how much they can produce. In illness it's not only the body that hurts — the feeling "I'm useless", imposed by a world that measures people by efficiency, hurts too. But a person's worth doesn't lie in their productivity. You are no less human when you are lying down, resting, accepting care. Allowing yourself to be vulnerable is also part of being human.
illness.practice: Tell yourself: "Today I am not labour power but a person, and my task is simply to be." Lie still for a minute, producing nothing, and note one thing you can thank your body for, even a tired one.

pride.text: In notes from 1844 Marx described what producing "as human beings" would be like: in my product I would see my individuality made visible, and I would enjoy it. What you are feeling now is exactly that enjoyment, and there's no need to hide it. The young Marx believed that a person unfolds in creative activity: in making something, they see themselves in what they have made. Free labour, for Marx, is not just a way to earn money but a way to realize your powers, to make them visible and tangible. Pride is a moment when you recognize yourself in what you've done: here are my efforts, my decisions, my strength, embodied in the world. It is the opposite of alienation. Allow yourself to enjoy this feeling without comparing yourself to others or belittling the result: it is yours.
pride.practice: Look at what you've made as into a mirror, and name aloud three of your qualities that are embodied in it.

quote.text: …and he therefore contemplates himself in a world that he has created.
quote.author: Karl Marx

melancholy.text: Every year Marx reread Aeschylus in the Greek, and at home the whole family quoted Shakespeare by heart. A quiet sadness, sorrow mixed with tenderness for what has gone, seems to have been familiar to him, and it doesn't need treating. In the Introduction to his manuscripts of 1857–1858 he asked a remarkable question: why does Greek art still give us pleasure? And he answered: the childhood of humanity holds an eternal charm for us as a stage that will never return. Melancholy is a similar feeling: we admire what was and will not come back, and it is precisely its unrepeatability that makes it beautiful. Melancholy is a way of cherishing the past without demanding that it return.
melancholy.practice: Read aloud a few lines of an old favourite poem or song — the way Marx reread his Greeks. Name what was unrepeatably beautiful about that time.
